title: Quiz: Tool Use & the Agent Loop

questions.prompt: Why can't a bare LLM check today's weather by itself?

options.text: Weather data is too complicated for language models
An LLM can only generate text — it has no ability to fetch data or run code; the surrounding app must do that
It can, as long as you ask politely

questions.explanation: The model is a text generator. To act on the world, the app offers it tools; the model requests a call, and the app executes it and feeds the result back.

questions.prompt: Put the agent loop in order: (1) app executes the tool and returns the result, (2) model requests a tool call, (3) model reads the result and decides next step, (4) app sends the user's task plus tool definitions.

options.text: 4 → 2 → 1 → 3, repeating from 2 until the model answers in plain text

questions.explanation: The app frames the task and available tools; the model proposes a call; the app runs it; the result re-enters the context; the model thinks again. The loop ends when the model responds with a final text answer instead of another tool call.

questions.prompt: In tool use, who actually runs the code — the model or the app?

options.text: The model runs it on the API provider's servers
The app runs it; the model only sends a structured request asking for the call
They each run it and compare results

questions.explanation: The model emits a structured 'please call X with these arguments' message. Execution — and therefore permissioning and safety — is entirely the app's job. This is why Claude Code can ask you before running a command.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real examples of the agent loop? (select all that apply)

options.text: Claude Code reading a file, editing it, then running the tests
A chatbot that answers purely from its training, with no tools
An AI assistant that searches the web, reads two pages, then writes a summary
This app's terminal exercises, where you watch tool names stream by as Claude works

questions.explanation: a, c, and d all cycle through think → act → observe. A tool-less chatbot (b) is a single model call — useful, but not an agent.
